title: Forces & Motion
description: Speed, velocity, acceleration, Newton's laws, forces, motion graphs, terminal velocity, and momentum.

notes.heading: Speed, Velocity and Acceleration
notes.body: Speed (scalar — magnitude only) = distance ÷ time. v = d/t (m/s). Velocity (vector — magnitude + direction): speed in a given direction. Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time. a = (v−u)/t (m/s²). Deceleration is negative acceleration. Distance-time graphs: gradient = speed. A straight line = constant speed; a horizontal line = stationary; a curve = acceleration (increasing gradient) or deceleration. Velocity-time graphs: gradient = acceleration; area under graph = distance travelled. A horizontal line = constant velocity; a sloping line = constant acceleration; a curve = changing acceleration. The area under a v-t graph can be found by splitting into shapes (rectangles, triangles).

illustration.alt: Distance-time and velocity-time graphs showing constant speed, stationary, acceleration, and deceleration.
illustration.caption: The gradient of a distance-time graph gives speed; the gradient of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration.

notes.heading: Newton's Three Laws of Motion
notes.body: First Law (Inertia): An object remains at rest or moves with constant velocity unless acted upon by a resultant (net) force. This is why seatbelts are needed — your body continues moving forward when the car stops. Second Law: F = ma. The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to its mass. Force measured in Newtons (N). 1 N = force needed to accelerate 1 kg by 1 m/s². Third Law: For every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force. These act on DIFFERENT objects. Rocket: gas pushed down → rocket pushed up. Walking: foot pushes ground back → ground pushes foot forward. Swimming: water pushed back → swimmer pushed forward.

illustration.alt: Illustrated examples of Newton three laws: seatbelt inertia, F equals ma rocket, and action-reaction in swimming.
illustration.caption: Newton First Law: objects remain at rest or move at constant velocity unless a resultant force acts.

notes.heading: Balanced and Unbalanced Forces
notes.body: Forces are vectors — they have magnitude and direction. The resultant (net) force is the vector sum of all forces. Balanced forces: resultant = 0 → object remains stationary or moves at constant velocity (Newton's 1st Law). Unbalanced forces: resultant ≠ 0 → object accelerates in direction of resultant force (Newton's 2nd Law). Free body diagrams show all forces acting on an object. Common forces: Weight (W=mg, downwards), Normal reaction (perpendicular to surface, upwards), Tension (in strings/ropes), Friction (opposes motion), Air resistance/drag (opposes motion, increases with speed), Upthrust (in fluids), Driving force (engine thrust).

illustration.alt: Free body diagrams showing balanced forces on a stationary box and unbalanced forces causing acceleration.
illustration.caption: When forces are balanced the resultant is zero; unbalanced forces cause acceleration.

notes.heading: Friction and Terminal Velocity
notes.body: Friction always opposes motion and converts kinetic energy to thermal energy. Air resistance (drag) increases with speed — as an object falls faster, drag increases until it equals weight. At this point: resultant force = 0 → no more acceleration → constant speed = terminal velocity. Skydiver: (1) Jump — weight > drag → accelerate downwards. (2) Drag increases with speed → acceleration decreases. (3) Weight = drag → terminal velocity (~200 km/h). (4) Parachute opens — drag suddenly >> weight → decelerate sharply. (5) New lower terminal velocity (~20 km/h) reached. Velocity-time graph shows: increasing curve → horizontal line → sharp deceleration → new lower horizontal line. Reducing drag: streamlined shapes (sports cars, aircraft, cyclists' helmets).

illustration.alt: Velocity-time graph of a skydiver showing acceleration, terminal velocity, parachute opening, and new lower terminal velocity.
illustration.caption: Terminal velocity is reached when drag equals weight and the resultant force becomes zero.

notes.heading: Mass, Weight and Gravity
notes.body: Mass (kg) — amount of matter in an object, constant everywhere. Weight (N) — gravitational force acting on mass. W = mg. On Earth, g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (often rounded to 10). On the Moon, g ≈ 1.6 m/s² → weight is ~1/6 of Earth weight but mass is unchanged. Centre of mass: point where weight appears to act. For uniform objects, it is at the geometric centre. Stability: an object topples when its centre of mass moves beyond its base. Wider base + lower centre of mass = more stable. Measured using a Newton meter (spring balance), which measures force, not mass (calibrated for Earth's g).

illustration.alt: Comparison of mass and weight on Earth vs the Moon, with W equals mg formula and centre of mass stability.
illustration.caption: Mass is constant everywhere; weight depends on the gravitational field strength (g).

notes.heading: Hooke's Law and Springs
notes.body: Hooke's Law: the extension of a spring is directly proportional to the applied force, up to the limit of proportionality. F = kx, where k = spring constant (N/m — stiffness), x = extension (m). A stiff spring has a high k. Beyond the elastic limit, the spring is permanently deformed (plastic deformation) and will not return to its original length. Force-extension graphs: straight line through origin = Hooke's Law obeyed. Curve = limit of proportionality exceeded. The area under the graph = work done (elastic potential energy stored). EPE = ½Fx = ½kx². Practical: hang masses on a spring, measure extension, plot F vs x. Gradient = k. Applications: suspension systems, measuring instruments (spring balances), elastic bands.

illustration.alt: Spring extension experiment setup and force-extension graph showing Hooke Law region and limit of proportionality.
illustration.caption: Hooke Law: extension is directly proportional to force up to the limit of proportionality (F equals kx).

notes.heading: Momentum
notes.body: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity: p = mv (kg·m/s). It is a vector quantity (direction matters). Conservation of momentum: in a closed system (no external forces), total momentum before a collision = total momentum after. Types of collisions: elastic — kinetic energy conserved (ideal, rarely perfectly in real life). Inelastic — kinetic energy NOT conserved (converted to heat/sound/deformation). Example: Car A (1000 kg, 20 m/s) hits stationary Car B (800 kg). They stick together (inelastic). Momentum before = 1000×20 = 20,000 kg·m/s. After: combined mass = 1800 kg. 20,000 = 1800×v → v ≈ 11.1 m/s. Safety features: crumple zones, airbags, and seatbelts increase collision time → reduce force experienced (F = Δp/Δt). The same change in momentum over a longer time = smaller force.

illustration.alt: Conservation of momentum diagram showing two cars colliding and sticking together, with before and after calculations.
illustration.caption: Momentum is conserved in a closed system: total momentum before collision equals total momentum after.

questions.stem: Car travels 150 m in 10 s. Average speed?
questions.explanation: Speed = distance/time = 150/10 = 15 m/s.

questions.stem: 4 kg object, resultant force 20 N. Acceleration?
questions.explanation: F=ma → a=F/m = 20/4 = 5 m/s².

questions.stem: Skydiver at terminal velocity. Forces are:
questions.explanation: Terminal velocity → zero acceleration → zero resultant force → forces balanced (Newton's 1st).

questions.stem: Rocket expels gas downward. Rocket moves:
questions.explanation: Action: gas pushed down. Reaction: rocket pushed up. Forces act on different objects.

questions.stem: Weight of 12 kg object on Earth? (g=10 m/s²)
Spring extends 0.05 m under 10 N force. Spring constant?
Distance-time graph: horizontal line. What does this show?
questions.explanation: Horizontal line = distance not changing = stationary. Gradient = 0 = speed = 0.

questions.stem: V-t graph: area under graph represents:
questions.explanation: Area = velocity × time = distance. Split area into rectangles/triangles for curved graphs.

questions.stem: Truck (5000 kg, 10 m/s) hits stationary car (1500 kg). They stick. Final speed?
Why do airbags reduce injury?
choices: They increase collision time → reduce force (F=Δp/Δt)
questions.explanation: Same change in momentum over a longer time = smaller average force = less injury.

questions.stem: 65 kg astronaut: weight on Moon? (g_moon=1.6 m/s²)
questions.explanation: W=mg=65×1.6=104 N. Mass is still 65 kg everywhere.

questions.stem: V-t graph: horizontal line at +15 m/s. What describes the motion?
questions.explanation: Horizontal v-t line = velocity not changing = constant velocity. No acceleration (gradient=0).

questions.stem: Spring stretched beyond elastic limit. What happens when force removed?
questions.explanation: Beyond elastic limit = permanent (plastic) deformation. The spring will not return to its original length.

questions.stem: Which increases friction between tyre and road?
choices: Rougher tyre tread and dry road
questions.explanation: Rougher surfaces = more friction. Wet conditions reduce friction (risk of aquaplaning). Tread channels water away.

questions.stem: A car accelerates from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 4 s. Acceleration?
questions.explanation: Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes. Using $a=(v-u)/t$, the car speeds up from $u=5\text{ m/s}$ to $v=25\text{ m/s}$ in $t=4\text{ s}$, so the change in velocity is $20\text{ m/s}$ and $a=20/4=5\text{ m/s}^2$. This means the car gains $5\text{ m/s}$ of speed every second, similar to a brisk family-car acceleration.

questions.stem: A runner covers 400 m in 50 s. Average speed?
questions.explanation: Speed = distance/time = 400/50 = 8 m/s. The distractors come from multiplying (400×50) or inverting (50/400) instead of dividing distance by time.

questions.stem: A 3 kg object experiences a resultant force of 12 N. Acceleration?
questions.explanation: F=ma → a=F/m = 12/3 = 4 m/s². 36 m/s² comes from multiplying force by mass; 0.25 m/s² from dividing mass by force.

questions.stem: A raindrop falls at a constant terminal velocity. Which statement about the forces on it is correct?
choices: Weight is greater than air resistance
Air resistance is greater than weight
Weight equals air resistance — resultant force is zero
No forces act on the raindrop
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so by Newton's 1st law the resultant force is zero: weight and air resistance are balanced.

questions.stem: A swimmer pushes the water backwards with her hands. What happens to the swimmer?
choices: She is pushed forwards — the water pushes back with an equal and opposite force
questions.explanation: Newton's 3rd law: pushing the water backwards (action) means the water pushes the swimmer forwards (reaction). The two forces act on different objects.

questions.stem: Weight of a 7 kg bag on Earth? (g=10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: W=mg = 7×10 = 70 N. 17 N comes from adding m and g; 0.7 N from dividing instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: A spring extends 0.02 m under a 5 N force. Spring constant?
questions.explanation: k=F/x = 5/0.02 = 250 N/m. 0.1 N/m is F×x and 0.004 N/m is x/F — both use the wrong operation.

questions.stem: Distance-time graph: a straight line sloping upwards. What does this show?
questions.explanation: A straight sloping line has a constant gradient, and gradient = speed, so the object moves at constant speed. Only a curve shows acceleration.

questions.stem: A velocity-time graph shows a horizontal line at 10 m/s for 6 s. Distance travelled in that time?
questions.explanation: Distance = area under a v-t graph = velocity × time = 10×6 = 60 m. 16 m comes from adding instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: A 1200 kg van moving at 15 m/s hits a stationary 800 kg car. They stick together. Final speed?
questions.explanation: Momentum before: 1200×15 = 18,000 kg·m/s. After: (1200+800)×v = 2000×v, so v = 18,000/2000 = 9 m/s. 22.5 m/s uses the car's mass alone; 15 m/s ignores the extra mass.

questions.stem: Crumple zones in a car reduce injury because they:
choices: Increase the collision time, so the same momentum change produces a smaller force
questions.explanation: F=Δp/Δt: crumple zones lengthen the collision time, so the same change in momentum happens with a smaller average force on the passengers.

questions.stem: An 80 kg astronaut stands on Mars, where g=3.7 m/s². His weight is:
questions.explanation: W=mg = 80×3.7 = 296 N. His mass is still 80 kg everywhere; 800 N would be his weight on Earth (g=10), and 21.6 N comes from dividing by g.

questions.stem: A spring is stretched beyond its limit of proportionality. On its force-extension graph, this region appears as:
choices: A straight line through the origin
A curve where extension increases faster than force
questions.explanation: The straight-line region is where Hooke's Law applies; beyond the limit of proportionality the graph curves as the extension grows faster than the force.

questions.stem: Which change would REDUCE the friction between a sled and the snow?
choices: Smoothing and waxing the sled's runners
Riding over gravel instead of ice
questions.explanation: Smoother surfaces slide more easily, so smoothing and waxing the runners reduces friction. Rougher surfaces and gravel increase grip.

questions.stem: A cyclist slows from 12 m/s to 4 m/s in 2 s. Acceleration?
questions.explanation: a=(v-u)/t = (4-12)/2 = -4 m/s². The negative sign means deceleration; dropping the sign slip gives the 4 m/s² distractor.
